An exponential moving average updates a running value using a fixed fraction of the new observation.
The update has the same algebra for different objects, but its interpretation depends on what is being averaged.
It is useful when recent history should influence a running estimate without storing every past value.

## The update and its object {#ema}

An EMA is a [recurrence]{.term key="recurrence"} defining a new sequence $m_t$ from observations $v_t$ and an initial value $m_0$.
All values must have compatible dimensions and represent the same quantity.
For a fixed decay coefficient $\rho$, it uses

$$
  m_t=\rho m_{t-1}+(1-\rho)v_t,
  \qquad 0\leq\rho<1.
$$

Older observations receive [geometrically decaying weights]{.term key="geometric-decay"}, with an initialisation contribution until it decays or is corrected.
The averaged object matters: model weights, a teacher's weights, losses, and action predictions are different objects.
[DINO](../../literature-review/vision/dino.qmd) averages teacher parameters.
[ACT temporal ensembling](../../literature-review/action/act.qmd#temporal-ensembling-uses-a-common-target-time) combines predictions for a common execution time and uses its own age convention.

## How past values contribute {#weights}

For a fixed decay $\rho$, unrolling the update gives

$$
  m_t=\rho^t m_0
  +(1-\rho)\sum_{j=1}^{t}\rho^{t-j}v_j.
$$

The latest value has weight $1-\rho$, and each additional step into the past multiplies its weight by $\rho$.
The initial value still contributes $\rho^t m_0$.
Thus, initialisation and the identity of the time index matter when comparing two averaging procedures.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: expand the recurrence"}

Substituting the previous update once gives

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  m_t={}&\rho^2m_{t-2}\\
  &+\rho(1-\rho)v_{t-1}+(1-\rho)v_t.
  \end{aligned}
$$

Repeating the substitution back to $m_0$ yields the visible sum.
The data weights sum to $1-\rho^t$, while the initialisation contributes the remaining weight $\rho^t$.

:::

## Interpreting an average in practice {#example}

With $\rho=0.9$, $m_0=0$, and a first observation $v_1=10$, the update gives $m_1=1$.
The result retains the initial value's weight; it does not imply that the first observation was close to one.
For a constant sequence $v_t=10$, the expansion gives $m_t=10(1-0.9^t)$.
If $m_0=0$, dividing by $1-\rho^t$ normalises the accumulated observation weights; this correction depends on that initialisation and the fixed-decay convention.

At $\rho=0$, the running value is simply the latest observation.
A value closer to one retains more history and responds more slowly to changes.
The index must be identified before comparing methods: training steps, arrival times, and a shared future execution time are not interchangeable.

## Connections {#connections}

An EMA of model parameters combines points along an [optimisation trajectory](optimization.qmd#gradient-descent), whereas an EMA of losses combines scalar measurements.
[DINO's teacher update](../../literature-review/vision/dino.qmd) uses the former, and [action horizons](../robotics/action-horizons.qmd) explains why overlapping action predictions need a specified execution time.
